row.name: Llyn Fawr
row.description: Llyn Fawr ('large lake' in Welsh) is a reservoir that occupies one of a series glacial cirques that form the northern escarpment of the South Wales Coalfield uplands, overlooking the heads of the Vale of Neath and the Cynon Valley [1]. It is known as the site of an important hoard of weapons and tools from the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age [1]. It lies on the northern flanks of Craig-y-Llyn [1]. Owing to its rapid and massive industrialisation during its coalfield boom, the Rhondda Valley, which lies on the south side of the escarpment, surpassed the supply of water it could source from its own river, so in 1909 the Water Works division of Rhondda Urban District Council contracted builders to convert Llyn Fawr into a reservoir [1]. Originally having an area of 11.927 acres, the lake was expanded, by the construction of a 25-foot high embankment dam and deepening of lake bed [1]. Bronze items included two cauldrons and axeheads [1]. The items appear to have been placed in the lake as votive offerings [1].

row.name: Apadana Castle Shush
row.description: The Palace of Darius in Susa was a palace complex that was built at the site of Susa during the reign of Darius I over the Achaemenid Empire [1]. The construction was conducted parallel to that of Persepolis [1]. Manpower and raw materials from various parts of the Achaemenid Empire contributed to its construction [1]. It was once destroyed by fire and was partially restored later; little has remained from the complex, which is today part of an archaeological site [1]. Construction works continued under Darius I's son, Xerxes, and to a lesser extent, Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC) and Darius II (423–404 BC) [1]. Artaxerxes II (404–358 BC) partially restored the palace as it was destroyed by a fire during the reign of Artaxerxes I fifty years earlier [1]. The apadana at Susa is similar to that of Persepolis, using the distinctive Persian column, topped by two bulls, which was probably developed here [1]. The Achaemenid constructions at Susa are mostly known through the royal inscriptions, which are mostly trilingual—in Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian [1].

row.name: Northwest Palace of Ashur-Nasir-Pal II
row.description: The Northwest Palace at Nimrud (ancient Kalhu) in Iraq was built by Neo-Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II (r. 883-859 BC) as part of his transformation of Nimrud into the imperial capital [1] [2]. The palace featured hundreds of carved gypsum ('Mosul marble') relief panels depicting royal hunts, warfare, and protective spirits, with the 'Standard Inscription' repeating the king's titles in cuneiform [1] [2] [3] [4]. Monumental lamassu -- winged human-headed bulls with five legs -- guarded its entrances [5] [6].

row.name: Machaquila
row.description: Machaquila (or Machaquilá, using Spanish orthography) is a major ruined city of the Maya civilization in what is now the El Peten department of Guatemala [1]. Machaquila is situated on the banks of the lower Machaquila River, which is a major tributary of the Pasión River [1]. During the Classic period, the city's location would have placed it upon a trade route running from the Maya Mountains in the east to the Pasión River in the west, and ultimately to the Usumacinta River [1]. Machaquila flourished in the Late to Terminal Classic periods, reaching the height of its power in approximately the ninth century [1]. The principal architecture at Machaquila has been dated to the Late Classic period, and includes temples and palace complexes [1]. Machaquila is unusual in the local region in lacking both an E-Group astronomical complex, and a ballcourt, which are both architectural arrangements that are often found in neighbouring cities [1]. Machaquila is not particularly notable for its architecture or size, rather for its abundant sculpted monuments [1].

row.name: Yanaque - Quilcamarca
row.description: Yanaque-Quilcamarca is an archaeological complex of two adjacent hilltop settlements at 3,820 meters elevation in Ancash Region, Peru (Ocros Province, Acas District) [1] [2]. Stone structures with clay mortar span from summit to slopes, featuring rectangular and semicircular forms reaching up to 2 meters in height [2]. According to local legend, a woman called Pichanamaria swept through the streets with a broom, causing an illness that killed the inhabitants of both villages, which had disputed a water source [2].

row.name: Batán Grande
row.description: The Batán Grande or Sicán Archaeological Complex, just north of Chiclayo, Ferreñafe province, Lambayeque region, Peru, is an ancient archaeological site that was occupied by the Sicán culture [1]. The site has 50 identified pyramids [1]. The archaeological site is located in the Historic Forest Sanctuary of Pómac [1]. The Lambayeque were a subdivision of the Sican, and appear first in the Batán Grande area [1].

row.name: Heroon of Trysa
row.description: The Heroon of Trysa is the modern name for an ancient tomb, built around 380 BCE in Trysa, in ancient Lycia in southwest Turkey [1]. It was discovered in 1841 by the gymnasium teacher Julius August Schönborn during his field research in Lycia [1]. The figural frieze originally consisted of c. 152 plates, which decorated the square outer wall of the tomb [1]. They are currently in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, where they were brought in 1882 after excavations by Otto Benndorf and Felix von Luschan [1].

row.name: Kow Swamp Archaeological Site
row.description: The Ghow Swamp Aboriginal Place, also known as the Kow Swamp archaeological site, is a protected Aboriginal place [1]. The archaeological site contains the largest known single population of human skeletal remains from the late Pleistocene era [1]. The remains are situated within the lunette of the eastern rim of a former wetland known as Ghow Swamp, in the North Central region of Victoria, Australia [1]. The site is 10 kilometres south-east of Cohuna in the central Murray River valley and is significant for archaeological excavations by Alan Thorne between 1968 and 1972 which recovered the partial skeletal remains of more than 22 individuals [1]. Following a campaign by Aboriginal community groups to have human remains repatriated from Australian and overseas museum collections, Museum Victoria returned the Ghow Swamp skeletons in 1990 to the Yorta Yorta people at Echuca who re-interred them [1]. Despite extensive reconstruction, the Ghow Swamp material was extremely fragmentary, with only two of the crania, KS1 and 5, being relatively complete [1].

row.name: Domus De Janas Torre Argentina
row.description: The domus de janas of Torre Argentina is a prehistoric and protohistoric tomb standing in one of the localities of the Sardinian municipality of Bosa, which counts at least thirty-six of them [1]. The Torre Argentina tomb belongs to the Sardinian class of domus de janas, pre-Nuragic rock-cut chamber tombs laid out like houses [1] [2].

row.name: Getic Burial Complex
row.description: The Getic burial complex is an archaeological site near Sveshtari in Razgrad Province in Bulgaria [1]. Various artifacts have been recovered from a Thracian tomb which dates from the beginning of the third century BC [1]. Another tomb, the Omurtag mount, has been linked to Cothelas, king of the Getae [1]. It is in the same area as the world heritage site Tomb of Sveshtari [1].

row.name: Niedertiefenbach - Megalithic Tomb
row.description: The Niedertiefenbach tomb (Steinkistengrab von Niedertiefenbach) is a gallery grave located near the village of Niedertiefenbach in Hesse, Germany [1]. Belonging to the Wartberg culture of Central Europe's Later Neolithic, it holds particular significance for its sequence of collective burial layers [1].

row.name: Ponte Emilio
row.description: The Pons Aemilius (Ponte Rotto) is the oldest Roman stone bridge in Rome, originally built in wood and rebuilt in stone in the 2nd century BC [1] [2]. It spanned the Tiber, connecting the Forum Boarium (the Roman cattle market) on the east bank with Trastevere on the west [1]. Today, only a single arch survives in the middle of the river, which gives the bridge its name Ponte Rotto ("Broken bridge") [1].

row.name: Tambo Viejo
row.description: Tambo Viejo is an archaeological site that extends over approximately 44 hectares (110 acres) in the north of the Arequipa region of southern Peru [1]. The site presents evidence of human occupation from the Early Intermediate period, including examples of Early Nasca pottery, to structures of the Inca period and remains from the Spanish colonial period [1]. Tambo Viejo is oriented in a north–south direction [1]. The main area on its north side is a large rectangular plaza, known as Plaza Principal or Plaza 1 [1]. The southern part of Tambo Viejo is made up of a labyrinth of structures connected to a smaller, more central plaza (Plaza 2), around which there are rectangular structures of various sizes [1].

row.name: Knockmaree Dolmen
row.description: Knockmaree Dolmen, or Knockmaree Cist, is a prehistoric site of the Neolithic period, in Phoenix Park just north of Chapelizod, near Dublin, Ireland [1]. The tomb, situated on a small ridge, is a cist, a type of burial chamber found in Ireland on the south and east coast [1]. It dates from about 3000 B.C. to 2500 B.C. A capstone, measuring 1.96 metres (6 ft 5 in) by 1.05 metres (3 ft 5 in), is supported by smaller stones [1]. The capstone is water-worn, and is thought to have come from the River Liffey nearby [1]. It was discovered in 1838, when workmen were employed to remove a tumulus of height 15 feet (4.6 m) and circumference 120 feet (37 m) [1]. In the centre of the mound were found the stones now visible; four other cists were found in the outer area [1]. The remains were examined by the Royal Irish Academy, the Academy's report later being delivered by George Petrie [1].

row.name: Spathes
row.description: Among the first archaeological sites discovered in Mount Olympus was the excavation site Spathes [1]. It is a necropolis from the Late Bronze Age [1]. Many of the burial offerings were made in the Mycenaean style, so that the Mycenaean cultural circle probably also extended over the border of Thessaly to Pieria [1]. The excavations brought to light 34 tombs, which were partly destroyed and plundered [1]. The most important finds were made in a tomb, in which apparently high ranking personalities were buried [1]. Remnants of a spear, a bronze sword, painted and unpainted vases and perfume bottles, jewelry and stone seals (partly with animal motifs) were discovered [1].

row.name: King Lud's Entrenchments and The Drift
row.description: King Lud's Entrenchments and The Drift is a 23.9 hectares biological Site of Special Scientific Interest which straddles the border between Lincolnshire and Leicestershire, and is east of Croxton Kerrial [1]. King Lud's Entrenchments is a scheduled monument [1]. King Lud's Entrenchments is also known as King Lud's Intrenchments or King Lud's Banks [1]. The site has not been excavated and its date is unknown [1]. It has been thought of as a Saxon boundary ditch, but aerial photographic work has suggested that it may be part of an extensive prehistoric boundary system extending from Northamptonshire to the Humber and termed `the Jurassic spine' [1]. This site has limestone grassland with tor-grass, cock's foot, crested dog's-tail and red fescue [1].

row.name: Jordan Hill Roman Temple
row.description: Jordan Hill Roman Temple is a Romano-Celtic temple and Roman ruin situated on Jordan Hill above Bowleaze Cove in the eastern suburbs of Weymouth in Dorset [1]. Original amateur archaeological excavations on the site were carried out by J. Medhurst in 1843-6 [1]. The floorplan of the temple measured 6.8 square metres [1]. The surrounding precinct measured 84 square metres and contained numerous deposits of animal bones, ceramics, and coins [1]. The site also includes a cemetery containing both cremations and inhumations [1].

row.name: Louloudies
row.description: An early Byzantine fortified episcopal complex in Pieria, northern Greece, built in the last quarter of the 5th century on the road between Thessaloniki and Larissa [1] [2]. The 80 x 90 m walled compound housed a three-aisled basilica and the bishop's residence, surrounded by walls with four rectangular corner towers and a double western gate [1]. The bishop of Pydna resided here, and the complex was expanded [1]. An earthquake in the mid-6th century destroyed the buildings; the site was later used as a cemetery before final abandonment in the 7th century following barbarian attacks [1].

row.name: Ameny Qemau Pyramid
row.description: The pyramid of Ameny Qemau is an ancient Egyptian pyramid located in southern Dahshur [1]. It was constructed for Ameny Qemau, an obscure king of the 13th Dynasty during the Second Intermediate Period [1]. The pyramid originally stood 35 metres high with a base length of 52 metres [1]. The stone constituting its upper structure has been entirely robbed but the damaged substructures remain [1]. The pyramid of Ameny Qemau was rediscovered in 1957 by a team led by Charles Arthur Musès [1]. In 1968, Vito Maragioglio and Celeste Rinaldi investigated the architecture of the pyramid [1]. More recently, the remains of the funerary equipment of the king were published by Nabil Swelim and Aidan Dodson [1].

row.name: Eightercua Stone Row
row.description: Eightercua is thought to originate from around 1700 BC, and by tradition is the burial place of Scéine, wife of the leader of the Milesian invaders, Amergin mac Míled [1]. The site features four tall slabs from 1.8 to 3 meters high running east and west [1]. From one stone a slab runs south and could be part of a tomb chamber or cist set in an oval cairn 1 meter high [1].

row.name: Kulubá
row.description: Kulubá is an ancient Maya civilization city and archeological site in Mexico [1]. It is located in Tizimín Municipality, northeast Yucatan [1]. The site contains a palace, an altar, ruins of two residences, and a round structure believed to be an oven [1]. The palace measures 6 metres tall, 55 metres long and 15 metres wide, and is believed to have been inhabited between 600-1050 CE [1]. A 1,000-year old Maya palace was discovered in Kulubá in 1939, by American archeologist Wyllys Andrews [1]. Kulubá consists of three main architectural structures [1]. They are believed to be residential sets of important lineages [1]. The site is about 6 kilometres in diameter and some 300 smaller structures had been discovered by 2009 [1].

row.name: La Corona
row.description: La Corona is the name given by archaeologists to an ancient Maya court residence in Guatemala's Petén department that was discovered in 1996, and later identified as the long-sought "Site Q", the source of a long series of unprovenanced limestone reliefs of exceptional artistic quality [1]. The site's Classical name appears to have been Sak-Nikte' ('White-Flower') [1]. During the 1960s, looted Maya reliefs from a then-unknown city surfaced on the international art market [1]. In 2005 Marcello A. Canuto, then a Yale professor, found a panel in situ at La Corona that mentioned two Site Q rulers [1]. In April 2012, La Corona Archaeological Project discovered a row of 12 staircase risers with many different relief scenes; another 10 sculpted risers were found looted from their original context but then discarded for being too eroded to be worth selling on the illicit antiquities market [1]. In 679 AD, a daughter of Calakmul's powerful Yuknoom Ch'een was given in marriage to a La Corona king [1]. In 721 AD, a daughter of the Calakmul king (Yuknoom Took' K'awiil) was married off to a king of La Corona [1].

row.name: Welsh Road
row.description: The Welsh Road, also known as the Welshman's Road or the Bullock Road, was a drover's road running through the English Midlands, used for transporting cattle from North Wales to the markets of South East England [1]. Drovers and their herds would follow the line of Watling Street from Shrewsbury and over Cannock Chase to Brownhills, from where the Welsh Road ran through Stonnall, Castle Bromwich, Stonebridge, Kenilworth, Cubbington, Offchurch, Southam, Priors Hardwick, Boddington, Culworth, Sulgrave, Syresham, Biddlesden, and Buckingham [1]. The age of the route is not known [1]. The parish records of Helmdon record money being given in 1687 "to a poor Welshman who fell sick on his journey driving beasts to London", but many lengths of the road coincide with parish or manorial boundaries, suggesting that it probably formed an ancient trackway dating to the pre-Roman era [1]. The northern section of the route from Brownhills to Stonebridge was made a turnpike by the Broughton, Chester and Stonebridge Turnpike Trust in 1759 [1].

row.name: Maiden Bower Hill Fort
row.description: Maiden Bower is a multi-period hillfort and causewayed enclosure near Dunstable in Bedfordshire, England, dating from the Neolithic to the Iron Age [1] [2]. The site, a scheduled monument, features a single rampart reaching up to 3 metres (9.8 ft) in height, surrounding a roughly circular enclosure approximately 225 metres (738 ft) in diameter [1]. A disused chalk quarry on the northwestern side has destroyed about 100 metres (330 ft) of the rampart [1] [2]. Archaeological evidence includes traces of a Neolithic causewayed enclosure beneath the Iron Age fortification [1] [2].

row.name: Thornborough Henges
row.description: The Thornborough Henges are an ancient monument complex that includes the three aligned henges that give the site its name [1]. They are located on a raised plateau above the River Ure near the village of Thornborough in North Yorkshire, England [1]. The site includes many large ancient structures including a cursus, henges, burial grounds and settlements [1]. They are thought to have been part of a Neolithic and Bronze Age 'ritual landscape' comparable to Salisbury Plain and date from between 3500 and 2500 BC [1]. The cursus is the oldest and largest ancient monument at Thornborough [1]. It is almost a mile in extent and runs from Thornborough village, under the central henge and terminates close to the River Ure in a broadly east/west alignment, 8 kilometres north-west of Ripon [1]. The three henges are almost identical in size and composition, each having a diameter of approximately 240 metres and two large entrances situated directly opposite each other [1].

row.name: Thul Hairo Khan
row.description: The Thul Hairo Khan is a Buddhist stupa, built possibly between the 5th and 7th centuries CE near the modern-day town of Johi, in Sindh, Pakistan [1]. It was constructed using cheroli and mud mortar to combine mud bricks and baked bricks [1]. The stupa is 50 feet high and 30 feet wide in size [1]. The stairs on the north side of the stupa lead to its top [1]. The stupa has an arched tunnel from north to south at ground level [1]. The construction of Thul Hairo Khan is of a rectangular type [1]. The round top of the stupa measures 5 feet 11 inches with a circumference of 14 feet [1].

row.name: Los Pinchudos
row.description: Los Pinchudos is an elaborate Chachapoya tomb complex, perched in a high rock cleft in one of Peru's northern Andean cloud forests [1]. The clay and stone tombs of the complex have wooden roofs and are painted in red, yellow, black, and white colors [1]. Anthropomorphic carvings featuring prominent phalluses are responsible for giving the site its name [1]. Los Pinchudos is located very near the related site of Gran Pajaten [1].

row.name: Castleshaw Roman Fort
row.description: Castleshaw Roman fort was a castellum in the Roman province of Britannia [1]. The remains of the fort are located on Castle Hill on the eastern side of Castleshaw Valley at the foot of Standedge but overlooking the valley [1]. The fort was constructed in c. AD 79, but fell out of use at some time during the 90s [1]. It was replaced by a smaller fortlet, built in c. 105, around which a civilian settlement grew [1]. The site has been the subject of antiquarian and archaeological investigation since the 18th century, but the civilian settlement lay undiscovered until the 1990s [1]. The location of the fort's granary, stables, the principia, the praetorium, and six long narrow buildings which are possibly workshops or storerooms are all known [1]. After being abandoned by the Romans, Castleshaw was rediscovered by antiquarian Thomas Percival in 1752 [1]. The fort was rectangular in shape and had sides of 115 metres and 100 metres, covering an area of approximately 1.2 hectares [1].

row.name: Pigi Athinas
row.description: Pigi Athinas (Source of Athena) is an archaeological site at the eastern foot of Mount Olympus near Platamonas, Greece, with evidence of human presence from the 7th millennium BC [1] [2]. A Neolithic settlement with successive occupation phases was established, yielding finds including a female figurine [3]. During the Bronze Age (c. 1620-1500 BC), a monumental tumuli cemetery was created with circular and elliptical burial mounds containing 17 individuals aged 20-50, interred with pottery grave goods [1] [3]. The tumuli expansion is associated with the spread of Indo-European peoples from the Eurasian steppes to the Balkans [3]. Rescue excavations began in 1999 under the Greek Ephorate of Antiquities [2].

row.name: Bant's Carn
row.description: Bant's Carn is a Bronze Age entrance grave located on a steep slope on the island of St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly, England [1]. The tomb is one of the best examples of a Scillonian entrance grave [1]. The tomb measures around 8 metres (26 ft) in diameter and stands on a low platform 12 metres (39 ft) across [1]. The entrance is 4.5 metres (15 ft) long and 1 metre (3.3 ft) high, with no roof [1]. It is separated from the burial chamber by a jamb [1]. The chamber itself measures around 5 metres (16 ft) in length and 1.5 metres (4.9 ft) in width and height, with four large capstones serving as a roof [1]. The tomb was excavated in 1900 by archaeologist, George Bonsor [1].

row.name: Poundbury Hill
row.description: Poundbury Hill in Dorset, England, is a multi-period archaeological site spanning Neolithic to Roman times [1]. It features a substantial Bronze Age occupation site and an Iron Age hillfort with late Iron Age burials [1]. The site includes a section of Roman aqueduct and, on its eastern side, an earlier Romano-British farmstead [1]. An extensive cemetery belonging to the Roman town Durnovaria has been identified [1].

row.name: Pike Hill Signal Tower
row.description: Pike Hill Signal Tower was one of a number of signal stations that were built on high ground overlooking the line of the Roman Stanegate road in northern Britannia during the early 2nd century [1]. It later became incorporated into Hadrian's Wall [1]. Its remains, a 2-metre long fragment of the south-east wall, lie south of a modern road cutting and field wall, located in the parish of Waterhead in Cumberland [1]. The station at Pike Hill signalled to two nearby stations, Gillalees Beacon and Barrock Fell [1]. Archaeological investigations have shown that the tower was built prior to either the turf or stone walls that exist nearby [1]. The tower was offset from the wall and stood at an angle of 45° to the line of the wall [1]. The signal tower was a square structure measuring around 6 metres on each side [1].

row.name: Broadsands Chambered Tomb
row.description: The Broadsands Chambered Tomb is a Neolithic burial chamber located on a slope overlooking Broadsands Beach in Torbay in Devon [1]. The tomb is currently a part of a hedge bank, situated on hilly farmland between Broadsands Beach and the tracks of the Dartmouth Steam Railway [1]. The tomb comprises a megalithic chamber and has a single entrance passageway [1]. It was originally set within a cairn, part of which survives to the present day [1]. During excavations it was found to contain the fragmentary remains of two adults and a child along with pottery shards from the Neolithic era [1].

row.name: Castallack Round
row.description: Castallack Round or Roundago is a prehistoric site near Castallack in Cornwall, England [1]. It is a scheduled monument [1]. The site is near the summit of a ridge overlooking the Lamorna valley [1]. Part of the rampart survives; it is composed of large stones and slabs, height about 1.6 metres and width 1.8 metres, forming an oval enclosure [1]. There was originally a surrounding ditch [1]. On the tithe map of 1840, the round is depicted as having a colonnade of stones leading from the entrance in the south to an inner circular enclosure; John Thomas Blight, describing it in 1865, found that these features had mostly disappeared [1]. To the north-west of the round there are thick stone walls, height up to 0.9 metres: the remains of a structure with an internal diameter of about 7.5 metres [1]. This is interpreted as a courtyard house, a type of building that developed in west Cornwall from the 2nd to 4th centuries AD [1].

row.name: Grottos of Juxtlahuaca
row.description: Juxtlahuaca, or Xiuxtlahuaca, is a cave and archaeological site in the Mexican state of Guerrero containing murals linked to the Olmec motifs and iconography [1]. Along with the nearby Oxtotitlán cave, Juxtlahuaca walls contain the earliest sophisticated painted art known in Mesoamerica, and only known example of non-Maya deep cave art in Mesoamerica [1]. The Juxtlahuaca site is located some 45 km southeast of the state capital Chilpancingo in what is now a National Park [1]. The entire cave system is slightly over 5 km [1]. The most well-known of the cave art is Painting 1, which features a large bearded man with a black cloak, a striped tunic, and an elaborate headpiece [1]. Also of note in Juxtlahuaca is a painting of a red Feathered Serpent with green plumes, near a red jaguar whose large ears and eyes give it a youthful cast [1]. A dozen skeletons have been found in the so-called Hall of the Dead [1].

row.name: Mahkeme Ağacin Kültürel Jeositi
row.description: Mahkeme Agacin is an underground cultural geosite near Kizilcahamam, 18 km from the district center north of Ankara, Turkey [1] [2] [3]. Carved into volcanic tuff, the multi-storey complex includes caves, rock-cut churches with carved crosses, dwellings, storage rooms, and a wine cellar [2] [4] [5].

row.name: Pilares do Lena
row.description: The Lena Pillars are dramatic natural rock formations along the Lena River in far eastern Siberia, Russia [1] [2]. Formed during the Cambrian period when this region was covered by ancient seas, the pillars represent exposed remnants of ancient sea basins [1]. The highest concentration of pillars is found between the villages of Petrovskoye and Tit-Ary [1]. The Lena Pillars Nature Park was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2012 [1] [2].

row.name: Kharrab Shams
row.description: Kharab Shams (also Kharab al-Shams) is an early Byzantine settlement located in the Dead Cities region of northwestern Syria [1]. The archaeological site is notable for its exceptionally tall basilica church, distinguished by its elevated columned arcades that led to its nickname 'Stelzenkirche' (stilted church) [1].

row.name: Tomba dei Giganti e Nuraghe Imbertighe
row.description: The Tomb of the Giants of Imbertighe is an archaeological monument located in the territory of Borore, Sardinia, Italy [1] [2] [3]. The site rises on the basaltic plateau of Abbasanta, an area rich in archaeological evidence in central Sardinia [1] [3] [4]. It is considered one of the most important sepulchral monuments on the island [1].

row.name: Xihuacan
row.description: Xihuacan is a Mesoamerican archaeological site on the Costa Grande of Guerrero, Mexico, near La Soledad de Maciel, Zihuatanejo and Petatlán [1]. Occupied for over 3,000 years by three distinct cultures, the site shows contact with the Teotihuacan and Olmec civilizations [1]. Earlier finds at the site include the King of La Chole stele and Mesoamerican ballcourt rings, though formal excavations only began recently [1].

row.name: Broch of Burrian
row.description: The Broch of Burrian is an Iron Age broch located on North Ronaldsay in the Orkney Islands [1]. The broch stands on a small headland next to a rocky shoreline [1]. The broch has an external diameter of 18 metres and an internal diameter of 9.5 metres [1]. The broch is surrounded by outer defences consisting of the remains of four concentric ramparts on the landward side [1]. The Broch of Burrian was excavated by William Traill, proprietor of the island, in 1870 and 1871 [1]. A large number of artefacts, including a significant quantity of worked bone objects, were discovered [1]. In addition, a number of artefacts of early historic or Pictish date were found [1]. These include a cross-slab with ogham inscription, painted pebbles and part of an iron bell of Celtic type [1].

row.name: Senegambian Stone Circles
row.description: The Senegambian Stone Circles are megalithic stone circles spanning The Gambia and Senegal, covering 30,000 km² with over 1,000 circles and tumuli arranged across a 350 km-long belt [1]. They represent the world's largest concentration of stone circles, used for over 1,500 years [1] [2]. They were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006 [1].

row.name: Marlborough Mound
row.description: The Marlborough Mound, also known as Merlin's Mound or Merlin's Mount, is a Neolithic monument in the town of Marlborough in the English county of Wiltshire [1]. Standing 19 metres tall, it is second only to the nearby Silbury Hill in terms of height for such a monument [1]. Since construction, the mound has functioned as the motte for a Norman castle, a garden feature for a stately home, and the site for a water tower within Marlborough College [1]. The mound is located on the western side of Marlborough within the grounds of Marlborough College, close to the River Kennet [1]. The original purpose of Marlborough Mound is unknown as it dates from around 2400 BC, the Neolithic period [1].

row.name: Waulud's Bank
row.description: Waulud's Bank is a possible Neolithic henge in Leagrave, Luton, England dating from 3000 BC [1]. Archaeological excavations in 1953, 1971 and 1982 date the site to around 3000 BC, in the Neolithic period, although there was evidence of earlier mesolithic hunter/fisher activity in the immediate area [1]. Waulud's Bank lies on a glacial ridge near which runs the prehistoric Icknield Way [1]. Initially it was probably a domestic enclosure used for cattle herding [1]. It has been suggested that it later became a henge monument, although the position of its surrounding ditch outside its timber-faced bank would be unusual [1]. The enclosure consists of a bank and external ditch of around 7 hectares with a turf-revetted chalk and gravel bank faced by a wooden stockade [1]. The bank stands 2.6 metres high in places; on the north side the excavated ditch was 9.2 metres wide and 2.1 metres deep [1]. Finds included neolithic pottery, animal bones and flint arrow heads, some on display at Stockwood Heritage Centre [1].

row.name: White Sheet Hill
row.description: White Sheet Hill, also known as Whitesheet Hill, is a hill in the English county of Wiltshire [1]. The hill is also the site of a Neolithic causeway camp and barrows; and an Iron Age hill fort [1]. The Roman road which runs along the hill was at one time the main route through the Selwood Forest [1].

row.name: Burnt Mound in Fox Hollies Park
row.description: The Burnt Mound in Fox Hollies Park is a Bronze Age archaeological feature in the Acocks Green area of south Birmingham, scheduled as an ancient monument in 2002 [1] [2]. The low oval mound stands approximately 0.3 metres high and measures 14 by 9 metres, composed of heat-crazed cobbles in gritty black soil [1] [3]. A geophysical survey revealed dense concentrations of stone along with at least seven probable pits, three hearths, and four troughs beneath the surface [3]. Burnt mounds, also known in Ireland as fulachtai fia, are thought to have been used primarily for cooking by heating stones to boil water in troughs, though some may have served as saunas [4] [5].

row.name: Fengbitou Archaeological Site
row.description: The Fengbitou Archaeological Site (鳳鼻頭遺址), officially Fengpitou (Chungkengmen), lies in Chungmen Village, Linyuan District, Kaohsiung, Taiwan, on a plateau [1]. The site covers 9.7 hectares and contains cultural layers dating to approximately 2,000–5,200 years ago [1]. Three prehistoric cultures are represented: Tapenkeng Culture, the Fengpitou Type of Niuchoutzi Culture, and Fengpitou Culture, demonstrating the prehistoric development of southwestern Taiwan [1].

row.name: Nakhchivan Rock Signs
row.description: The Nakhchivan Rock Signs were discovered in 2016 at Agsal, between the villages of Erefse and Milax in the Culfa (Julfa) region of Azerbaijan [1] [2]. Three rock signs were found featuring drainage channels directed towards the canyon, suggesting fluid flow [1]. Similar rock signs are common across Southern Azerbaijan and Eastern Anatolia [1] [3].

row.name: Hulbjerg Passage Grave
row.description: The Hulbjerg Passage Grave (Danish: Hulbjerg Jættestue) is a passage grave located at the southern end of the Danish island Langeland, situated on a 15-meter hill south of the ferry harbour Bagenkop [1]. Dating back to 3300–3200 BCE, it is part of the Neolithic Funnelbeaker culture [1]. The grave consists of a chamber and a separate lateral passageway [1]. The rectangular grave chamber is embedded in a round barrow of about 20 m diameter, framed by a ring of stones [1]. The walls of the 6.5 x 1.7 metre chamber consist of 13 large uprights, tightly compacted with a fine wall of hewn stone tiles [1]. On the southern wall of the chamber, vertical stone plates form a separate section [1]. In 1960, the grave was excavated by one of Europe's leading experts in late Stone Age burials, Håkon Berg of the Langeland Museum [1]. In the separate section in the grave chamber, sharpened flint axes and chisels, flint daggers, transverse arrowheads, decorated ceramics, amber beads as well as heaps of bones of 36 adults and 17 children were found [1].

row.name: Barrow Clump
row.description: Barrow Clump is an archaeological site in Figheldean parish, Wiltshire, England, about 3+1⁄2 miles north of the town of Amesbury [1]. Barrow Clump lies on the northwestern slope of rising ground about 700 metres east of the village of Ablington [1]. The surviving part of the monument is a bowl barrow about 30 metres in diameter [1]. The barrow was constructed in the early Bronze Age on the site of a Neolithic settlement, and much later, around the 6th century, it was re-used as an Anglo-Saxon cemetery [1]. Partial excavations were carried out in the 19th century, in the early 20th century by Lt Col William Hawley, and in 2003–2004 by English Heritage [1]. Permission was granted for full excavation in 2012–2014 in order to record the site, which was being extensively damaged by badgers [1]. Many Bronze Age items were found, with a smaller quantity from the Neolithic period [1]. Many Saxon graves were uncovered, together with items including a bucket-shaped drinking vessel, made from pieces of yew wood bound together with bronze [1].

row.name: Ahu Nau Nau
row.description: Ahu Nau Nau is a megalithic platform on Easter Island [1] [2] [3]. It occupies a site traditionally regarded as the birthplace of the island's history and culture [2] [4] [5]. According to oral tradition, this was the residence of high-ranking chiefs of the powerful Miru clan, and the landing place of the island's first king, Ariki Hotu Matu'a, who established the first settlement there with his people [2] [4] [5] [6].

row.name: Bluestonehenge
row.description: Bluestonehenge, also called Bluehenge, is a prehistoric henge and stone circle monument about 1 mile south-east of Stonehenge in Wiltshire, England [1]. Tentative dating places the monument between about 3000 and 2400 BC [1]. Excavations in August 2008 and again in August 2009 revealed several stone settings thought to have been erected between 3400 and 2500 BC [1]. The stone circle may have held as many as 27 stones within a diameter of 33 feet (10 m) [1]. The henge ditch and a series of stone settings are all that survives of the site, none of it visible above ground [1].

row.name: Duraz Temple
row.description: The Diraz Temple is a Dilmun-era religious structure in the village of Diraz, Bahrain [1] [2] [3]. Its central hall features cylindrical columns with a diameter of 120 cm arranged in two rows, nine of which survive to a height of 60 cm, along with a possible cella room containing an altar [3]. Partly explored by a British expedition in 1973-75 in cooperation with the Directorate of Archaeology, excavations yielded fragmentary clay vessels and two stamp seals in the classical Dilmun style [2] [3]. Its architectural design differs from both Mesopotamian temples and the nearby Barbar temple [3]. East of the temple, a later subterranean tomb dated to the Kassite period with Iron Age reuse was discovered [3].

row.name: Duropolis
row.description: Duropolis is the name of an archaeological site at Winterborne Kingston in the English county of Dorset, believed to be the remains of the first planned town in Britain [1]. The 32,000 square metres Iron Age settlement is believed to date to around 100 BCE, making it 70 years older than the Roman town of Silchester [1]. The site has been named by archaeologists after the Iron Age Durotriges tribe [1]. Its settlement may have been associated with the abandonment of nearby Maiden Castle in the 1st century BCE [1]. Found in July 2015 by students from Bournemouth University as part of the Durotriges Big Dig project, the remains of 16 Iron Age roundhouses have been excavated while geophysical survey shows a total of at least 150 roundhouses and other features in the area [1]. A number of animal skeletons discovered at the site suggest that the Iron Age Celtic population may have believed in hybrid-animal monster myths akin to those of the Mesopotamians, Ancient Greeks and Egyptians [1].

row.card: Duropolis in Dorset is believed to be Britain's first planned town. Remains of 16 Iron Age roundhouses were dug up, and animal skeletons may hint at a belief in hybrid-animal monster myths.

row.name: Barranc de Gàfols
row.description: The Barranc de Gàfols, also referred as Pomeralet, is an archaeological site in Ginestar, Catalonia [1]. It is one of the most important First Iron Age sites in Catalonia, since it presents a continuous occupation since the Last Bronze Age [1]. The site is located 1 km south of Ginestar, in the west bank of the river Ebro [1]. The site was first occupied during the Late Bronze Age, when cottages were established [1]. During the First Iron Age, relatively complex rectangular and trapezoid buildings were planned, with the creation of at least 17 households and 3 streets [1]. Some of these buildings correspond to private households, since a fireplace has been found in each one of the structures, except one which has been identified as a common building devoted to agricultural activities, due to the presence of stone mills [1]. In 1990, excavation works began in Gàfols and continued until 1998 [1].

row.name: Aslantepe Ruins
row.description: A 30-metre-high archaeological tell covering 4.5 hectares on the Malatya plain in eastern Turkey, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 [1] [2] [3]. Arslantepe's Late Chalcolithic palace complex (4th millennium BC) preserves evidence of early state formation and a bureaucratic system predating writing [1]. The site yielded the world's earliest known swords excavated by Marcella Frangipane of Sapienza University [1] [2].

row.name: Sechin Alto
row.description: Sechin Alto is a massive architectural complex in Peru belonging to the Early Formative period (2000-1500 BC) [1]. It is located in the Casma Province, the Ancash Region, on the left bank of the Sechín River [1]. Archaeologist Julio C. Tello was the first to make a thorough description of this archaeological site during his visit to the valley of Casma in 1937 [1]. The main structure, called "Templo", has a pyramidal shape [1]. It measures 350m by 300m, and reaches the height of 35m [1]. It consists of raised embankments and walls with large stones alternating with smaller ones; conical adobe bricks are seen in the interior [1]. In front of the "Templo" extend five courts or plazas, some with sunken circular courts; this indicates the ceremonial character of the whole complex [1]. The complex is oriented to the northwest, and its length is about 2 km [1].

row.name: Kudaro
row.description: Kudaro is a complex of Paleolithic cave sites in the highlands of Georgia, located at approximately 1,600 meters above sea level [1]. The caves contain Lower Paleolithic Acheulean artifacts including bifaces, choppers, and sidescrapers [1] [2] [3]. Radiothermoluminescent dating of the Acheulean layer (5c) yielded dates of 360,000 years ago [4]. The caves also yielded Middle Pleistocene vertebrate remains, including the Kudaro cave bear [5] [6].

row.name: Huaca Esmeralda
row.description: Huaca La Esmeralda is a Chimu culture archaeological site in Trujillo, Peru, located halfway between the city center and Chan Chan [1] [2]. The rectangular pyramid features two platforms measuring approximately 65 by 41 meters, accessible through central ramps [3]. Its walls display distinctive relief decorations depicting fishing nets with fish, seabirds, waves, and geometric diamond patterns [1] [2] [3]. Buried under sand, it was discovered by a local landowner in 1923 [2].

row.name: Turoe Stone
row.description: The Turoe stone is a 1.2 metre tall granite stone decorated in a Celtic style normally located in the village of Bullaun, County Galway, Ireland [1]. It probably dates to about the period 100 BC to AD 100 [1]. The Turoe stone is National Monument of Ireland Number 327 [1]. The top half of the stone is covered with a continuous abstract curvilinear La Tène style design similar to that on the Castlestrange Stone in County Roscommon [1]. The religious or ceremonial purposes of the stone are lost in time [1].

row.name: Monument of Aemilius Paullus
row.description: The Monument of Aemilius Paullus was erected in the Sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi shortly after 167 BCE in order to commemorate the Roman victory over King Perseus of Macedon at the Battle of Pydna [1]. It incorporated an incomplete pillar originally intended as a base for a portrait of King Perseus, which would have established the Macedonian presence in Delphi and reminded the Delphians of the tradition of friendship between them and the royal family [1]. The completed monument had a bronze equestrian statue that sat on top of a rectangular pillar over 9 meters high [1]. Deployed on all four sides at the top of the rectangular marble pillar is a relief frieze depicting the Battle of Pydna [1]. The frieze runs 6.5 meters long and 0.31 meters high [1]. The frieze is the earliest known example of Greek sculpture in a purely Roman context [1].

row.name: Mezine
row.description: Mezine (or Mezyn) is an Epigravettian archaeological site in northern Ukraine, located on the Desna River bank near the village of Mezine in Novhorod-Siverskyi Raion, Chernihiv Oblast [1] [2]. The site holds the most Paleolithic artifact finds in Ukraine [1]. It is known for a set of bracelets engraved with marks possibly representing lunar calendar cycles [1]. Also discovered at Mezine is the earliest known example of a meander pattern, found on an object carved from mammoth ivory to resemble a bird [1] [2] [3].

row.name: Rastrojón
row.description: Rastrojón is a Maya archaeological site in western Honduras [1]. It appears to be associated with the major Classical period city of Copán―the capital of a Maya kingdom that existed from 5th to 9th centuries CE―situated just two kilometres away [1]. The site was abandoned following the collapse of the Copán kingdom in 822; the site was constructed on top of a geological fault that made building difficult, so it may be that the inhabitants judged the location not worth the effort after the fall of the nearby royal centre [1]. Rastrojón was discovered in 1979, during a survey of the area around Copán [1]. From 2007 to 2013, the Rastrojón Archaeological Project, sponsored by Harvard University and the Honduran Institute of Anthropology and History undertook a programme of rescue archaeology and conservation at the site [1].

row.name: Broch of Borwick
row.description: The Broch of Borwick is an Iron Age broch located on Mainland, Orkney, Scotland [1]. The broch stands on top of a cliff-top promontory 20 metres above the sea [1]. The broch has an external diameter of 17 metres and an internal diameter of 8 metres [1]. The walls which are 3.5 to 5 metres thick currently stand to a maximum height of 2.6 metres [1]. The eastern half of the broch and the entrance passage are well preserved, but the western half has been destroyed by erosion [1]. The site was excavated in 1881 by W. G. T. Watt, and the interior was cleared of debris [1]. Finds included several combs, a small whale vertebra cup, a spindle whorl, a stone gaming piece, a whetstone, hammerstones, some stone knives and choppers, an iron rod, and some querns [1].

row.name: Bada Valley Megaliths
row.description: Palindo, Torompana, Tarae Roe, and Loga are some of the names given by locals to the ancient statues in the Bada Valley [1]. The megalithic statues in the Bada Valley represent human faces that have been stylized, where the eyebrows and nose are depicted as one, while the mouth is omitted [1]. The statues in the Bada Valley generally have clear gender markers [1]. On the Palindo and Meturu statues, male genitalia are carved [1]. On the Langke Bulawa statue, female genitalia are depicted [1]. Kalamba are artifacts in the form of large jars with lids, 1.5-2 meters in diameter, used for burial, found in the Bada Valley [1].

row.name: Round Loaf
row.description: Round Loaf is a Late Neolithic or Bronze Age tumulus on Anglezarke Moor in the West Pennine Moors near Chorley in Lancashire, England [1]. The bowl barrow is a scheduled monument considered to be of national importance [1]. Round Loaf is one of 10,000 bowl barrows constructed between the Late Neolithic period and the late-Bronze Age (2400 - 1500 BC) [1]. Round Loaf occupies a prominent landmark position on Anglezarke Moor [1]. The ancient monument includes an oval mound measuring 73 metres from north to south and 66 metres from east to west [1]. It is constructed of earth and small stones to a height of from 3.6 to 5.5 metres [1]. Flakes of flint have been found on the mound's summit [1].

row.name: Sussex Greensand Way
row.description: The Sussex Greensand Way is a Roman road that runs east-west linking the London to Lewes Way at Barcombe Mills to Stane Street at Hardham [1]. The road, which has almost entirely fallen out of use, follows the free draining ridge of greensand which lies north of the South Downs [1]. It is a planned route rather than a Romanised Iron Age track, following a few straight alignments without any steep gradients [1]. A number of important Roman villas and their farming estates were linked by the road [1]. It is not known at what time during the Roman period the road was built [1]. Sections made through some better-preserved parts of the road show it to have been of light construction with about 3 inches of metalling, usually on a low agger, but in drier places laid direct on the natural subsoil [1]. The width of metalling varies from 25 feet at the wider points, on an agger about 40 feet wide, down to 9 feet on terraceways crossing hillsides [1]. The metalling on this road has been found to be flint at all the points studied, with a camber of about 8 inches [1].

row.name: Sancreed Beacon
row.description: Sancreed Beacon is a Bronze Age archaeological site near the village of Sancreed in the Penwith peninsula of Cornwall maintained by the Cornwall Heritage Trust [1]. On top of the hill are several stone cists and Bronze Age archaeological remains comprising burial mounds and the remains of a Bronze Age hut on the Western slope [1]. This site can be taken in the context of a rich variety of archaeological evidence in the vicinity from the Iron Age, Bronze Age and dating as far back as Neolithic times including Carn Euny Iron Age village 1 mile to the southwest, Caer Bran Hill Fort half a mile southwest, Sancreed Holy Well to the southeast, and Bartinney Castle to the west about 1 mile [1].

row.name: Nausharo
row.description: Nausharo is an archaeological site dating back to the Harappan period, located in Balochistan, Pakistan [1]. The excavations were carried out between 1985 and 1996 by a French team of archaeologists, under the direction of Jean-François Jarrige [1]. Excavations at Nausharo, 6 km from Mehrgarh, revealed a dwelling-site contemporaneous and identical to the later periods of Mehrgarh [1]. The discovery of a pottery workshop at Nausharo revealed fired and unfired pottery pieces and unworked clay, as well as 12 flint blades or blade fragments [1]. Also significant was the discovery of copper traces found on the platforms of two blades examined with a scanning electron microscope and X ray analysis [1]. Somewhere between 2600 BC and 2000 BC, Mehrgarh seems to have been largely abandoned in favor of Nausharo, which became fortified and quite large [1].

row.name: Arch of Augustus
row.description: The Arch of Augustus is an Ancient Roman arch constructed in the city of Susa, Piedmont, in the province of Turin [1]. It was built in 9–8 BC to record the renewed alliance between Emperor Augustus and Marcus Julius Cottius, a Celto-Ligurian ruler who had been made king and Roman prefect of the Cottian Alps [1]. From above, the arch forms a rectangle 11.93 metres long and 7.3 metres wide [1]. It rests on two large bases and there is only one archway [1]. The entablature rests on four Corinthian columns placed at the extremities of each corner, such that a quarter of each drum is embedded in the monument [1].

row.name: Teotihuacan - Palace Atelelco
row.description: Palace Atetelco is an archaeological complex within the ancient city of Teotihuacán, located in the Valley of Mexico northeast of modern-day Mexico City [1] [2] [3]. The complex consists of multiple rooms arranged around courtyards, reflecting the urban planning typical of Teotihuacán's apartment compounds [3] [4].

row.name: Planetrees - Hadrian's Wall Section
row.description: (2nd c. AD) Planetrees is an extant section of Hadrian's Wall named after the farm located around 250 metres (820 ft) to the west [1] [2]. The surviving section is 35 metres (115 ft) in length [1]. The eastern part (approximately 20 metres/66 ft) is built as Broad Wall, 10 Roman Feet wide, while the western section (approximately 15 metres/49 ft) uses Narrow Wall construction at 8 Roman Feet wide, yet still on foundations originally installed for a Broad Wall [1].

row.name: Smythe's Megalith
row.description: Smythe's Megalith, also known as the Warren Farm Chamber, was a chambered long barrow near the village of Aylesford in the south-eastern English county of Kent [1]. Probably constructed in the 4th millennium BCE, during Britain's Early Neolithic period, it was discovered in 1822, at which point it was dismantled [1]. Built out of earth and at least five local sarsen megaliths, the long barrow consisted of a roughly rectangular earthen tumulus with a stone chamber in its eastern end [1]. Human remains were deposited into this chamber [1]. Archaeologists have established that the monument was built by pastoralist communities shortly after the introduction of agriculture to Britain from continental Europe [1]. Although representing part of an architectural tradition of long barrow building widespread across Neolithic Europe, Smythe's Megalith belonged to a localised regional variant produced in the vicinity of the River Medway, now known as the Medway Megaliths [1].

row.name: La Torre-La Janera Megalithic Site
row.description: The La Torre-La Janera megalithic site is located in the municipalities of Ayamonte and Villablanca in the province of Huelva, Andalusia [1]. It was discovered in 2018 when a farmer intended to prepare the land to cultivate avocados and in view of the archaeological potential of the site the local council demanded a survey to be made [1]. The megaliths are in about 90 hectares that are part of a 600 hectare large rural estate [1]. So far, 526 standing stones were revealed during the survey, either still standing or lying on the surface [1].

row.name: Anta da Estria
row.description: The Anta da Estria is a megalithic dolmen situated between Belas and Queluz in the Lisbon District of Portugal [1]. Based on datings of human remains, it is believed to date back to the Late Neolithic and early-Chalcolithic eras (4000-2500 BC) [1]. The Anta da Estria, the Anta do Monte Abraão and the Anta da Pedra dos Mouros are collectively known as the Antas de Belas, and were first identified in the 1870s by Carlos Ribeiro [1]. Carlos Ribeiro, who carried out research in early 1875 and published his results in 1880, described the tomb as having a polygonal chamber, 2–5 metres wide and 2.75 metres high, approached by a corridor bordered by small slabs of limestone [1]. Ribeiro identified nine raised slabs but did not identify any stones that could have formed a roof [1]. Limited artifacts have been discovered at the site but many are thought to have been removed prior to the discovery by Ribeiro [1]. Twelve arrowheads were identified, together with two bone artifacts and three small, almost-complete pots [1].

row.name: Dun Hallin
row.description: Dun Hallin is an Iron Age broch located near the northwest coast of the island of Skye, in Scotland [1]. Dun Hallin is located on the Waternish peninsula of Skye, just east of the settlement of Hallin [1]. It occupies the southeast end of a steep-sided rocky plateau overlooking a fertile valley and the sea [1]. Dun Hallin has an external diameter of around 17.4 metres and an internal diameter of around 10.5 metres [1]. The broch walls currently stand to a maximum height of 3.8 metres on the north and west sides [1]. The entrance is on the southeast side but is in a ruined state [1]. On each side of the entrance passage are oval guard cells, although only the northern, right-hand cell can easily be seen [1]. The interior of the broch has much rubble grassed over [1].

row.name: Brown Willy Cairns
row.description: The summit of Brown Willy is 1,378 feet above sea level, the highest point on Bodmin Moor and in the county of Cornwall [1]. Brown Willy Summit Cairn or Brown Willy North Cairn is a man made rock pile that sits alongside an Ordnance Survey triangulation station [1]. Brown Willy Summit Cairn has never been excavated and folklore suggests an ancient Cornish king may lie entombed underneath [1].

row.name: Roman Dam of Pego da Moura
row.description: The Roman Dam of Pego da Moura is a small buttress dam situated in the municipality of Grândola in the Setúbal District of Portugal [1]. The dam was constructed during the middle of the Roman occupation of Portugal [1]. Built in two phases, it consists of a rectilinear wall that was originally about 40 metres long [1]. The ruins have a maximum height of 3 m. and a thickness of 2.90 m [1]. There are six downstream buttresses that are 2.50 m. apart, which are around 2.70 m. thick and 2.90 m long [1]. The dam was almost entirely constructed using opus incertum [1]. The dam was first noted by Father Carvalho Costa in 1712 in his work, Corographia Portugueza [1]. However, it was not until the 1990s that a brief archaeological study was conducted [1].

row.name: Stele of Arniadas
row.description: The Stele of Arniadas is an Archaic-period funerary stele in Corfu, Greece, found on the tomb of Arniadas, a warrior [1]. It was intended to mark his grave and honour his memory by enumerating his bravery in a battle near the river Arachthos in the location of ancient Ambracia, modern-day Arta [1]. The stele was found in 1846 at the necropolis of the Corfu Palaiopolis in the suburb of Garitsa, near the Tomb of Menecrates, after a demolition of Venetian fortifications in the area by the British, who at the time ruled Corfu [1]. The date of the stele is early 6th century BC [1]. The stele bears an epigram written vertically in verses following an alternating direction writing style called boustrophedon [1]. The inscription describes the details of the death of warrior Arniadas in a battle near ships on the banks of the river Arachthos and praises the dead warrior's bravery [1]. The Homeric hexameter of the verses, the proximity of the battle to ships, and the pompous style of the writing are clear indications that the inscription was influenced by the writings of Homer [1].

row.name: Bolt Tail
row.description: Bolt Tail is a headland in Devon, England, immediately to the southwest of Hope Cove in the South Hams district [1]. Bolt Tail is the site of an Iron Age promontory fort, although little evidence now remains of this structure; it occupied a classic promontory defended from inland by a linear earthwork at some 60 metres above sea level [1].

row.name: Huntersquoy Chambered Cairn
row.description: Huntersquoy chambered cairn is a Neolithic chambered cairn located on the island of Eday, in Orkney [1]. Huntersquoy chambered cairn is situated on a gently sloping hill overlooking Calf Sound in Orkney, Scotland [1]. It is a good example of an Orkney–Cromarty chambered cairn [1]. It dates from the Neolithic era, sometime during the years 3000 through 2001 BC [1]. These tombs, often called "stalled cairns" are characterized by a central passage edged by upright stones which divide spaces into separate chambers [1]. Huntersquoy is unique in that it is a rare double-storied burial monument [1]. It is seen as a small, unobtrusive, circular mound, 10 m in diameter and 60 cm in height above ground [1].

row.name: Praia das Maçãs Prehistoric Monument
row.description: The Praia das Maçãs Prehistoric Monument, also known as the Tholos of Outeiro das Mós, consists of an artificial Neolithic cave and a Chalcolithic domed or beehive tomb [1]. The artificial cave was probably dug into the rock in the second half of the 4th millennium BC or early in the 3rd [1]. The Neolithic cave has a diameter of around 2 m and was originally covered with stone supports [1]. The later tholos was composed of a circular chamber with a diameter of approximately 5.5 m [1]. Walls were constructed with limestone slabs placed horizontally [1]. A pillar was raised in the centre to support a dome [1]. Items found at the site have included geometric microliths, arrowheads, polished axes, and cylindrical idols [1].

row.name: Poblat Talaiòtic de Talatí de Dalt
row.description: Talati de Dalt is a major Talayotic settlement on Menorca, Spain, located approximately 4 km from Mao [1] [2]. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage "Talayotic Menorca" designation, the site features a distinctive taula (T-shaped monument) with a unique leaning support column, hypostyle rooms, and sections of defensive walls [2] [3] [4] [5].

row.name: Alderman's Barrow
row.description: Alderman's Barrow is a Bronze Age bowl barrow on Exmoor, England, serving as a burial chamber and later a boundary marker for the parishes of Exford, Exmoor, Luccombe, and Porlock [1] [2]. The turf-covered mound measures 24 by 22 meters and stands 1.4 meters high [2]. Known as Osmunesburgh in the 13th century and Owlaman's Burrow in the 17th century, it received its current name in 1782 [1] [2]. It was scheduled as a protected monument in 1934 [1].

row.name: Borġ l-Imramma
row.description: The Borġ l-Imramma site is a major building of the temple period [1]. It is located 500 metres southeast of the Ta' Ċenċ plateau [1]. Near the structure, cart ruts and a dolmen can also be observed [1]. The temple shares some of the characteristics of the usual Maltese Megalithic temple such as the Ħaġar Qim or Ġgantija temples [1]. This design usually includes a large, roughly circular courtyard, about 20 metres across [1]. Clustered on its north, west and south sides are a number of small, again nearly circular chambers [1]. An entrance passage for the courtyard is on the northwest wall [1]. This passage is made from large, squared stones [1].

row.name: Riasc Monastic Settlement
row.description: Reask is a ruined early Monastic site located 1 km east of Baile an Fheirtéaraigh, County Kerry [1]. The remains of the site include the low remnants of buildings and enclosure walls and a cross-slab standing stone which sits in the middle of the compound [1]. Some of the artefacts found in the excavation at Reask, including some of the cross-inscribed stones, are on display in Músaem Chorca Dhuibhne [1]. The Reask Cross Pillar is similar to the pillars found nearby at Kilfountain and Kilmalkedar on the Dingle Peninsula [1]. The site is a National Monument in state care [1].

row.name: Xnaheb
row.description: Xnaheb is an archaeological site of the pre-Columbian Maya civilization, one of five primary sites identified in the southern Belize region [1]. The center is built on a ridge of foothills that extends from the Maya Mountains, in what is now the Toledo District of Belize [1]. Based on certain architectural similarities between the two sites, it is possible that Xnaheb was founded as an offshoot of Nim Li Punit [1].

row.name: Kobba Bent el Rey
row.description: Kobba Bent el Rey is a vaulted underground construction, located on the hill of Bordj Djedid within Carthage, Tunisia [1]. Also known as the Baths of Dido, the structure was deliberately built below ground level [2] [3]. Its rooms feature a rich variety of vault types including tunnel vaults and domes in combinations of smaller and larger cupolas, constructed using lost formwork from earthenware pipes coated in Roman concrete [3] [4]. It is considered the best-preserved residential monument at the site of Carthage [1].

row.name: Hadnmauer
row.description: The Hadnmauer is the protected ruin of a letzi (defensive barrier across a valley) in the Gailtal valley in Austria, dating to the Late Antiquity [1]. It runs from Rattendorf to Jenig [1]. Originally 1.6 kilometres long, only 336 metres survive [1]. On its western side, rooms for the defending personnel are discernible [1].

row.name: Acatitlan
row.description: Acatitlan is an archaeological zone located in the town of Santa Cecilia, in the municipality of Tlalnepantla de Baz in the State of Mexico, about 10 km northwest of modern Mexico City [1] [2]. In pre-Columbian times, this temple complex was situated on the northwest shore of the great Lake Texcoco [1] [3].

row.name: Nine Maidens Stone Row
row.description: Nine Maidens stone row is an ancient monument in the parish of St Columb Major, Cornwall, England [1]. The Nine Maidens are also known in Cornish as Naw-voz, or Naw-whoors meaning "the nine sisters" [1]. This late neolithic stone row is 2 miles north of St Columb Major [1]. The row comprises nine stone megaliths and is situated in a field alongside the A39 between St Columb Major and Wadebridge [1]. The row is approximately 108 metres long, with stones varying in height from 0.8 metres to 2.1 metres [1]. The stones are irregularly spaced and aligned in a north easterly direction [1]. They are aligned towards a stone known as the Fiddler, which lies on the moorland approximately 800 metres away [1]. The stone row was first noted by historian Richard Carew in 1605 [1].

row.name: Highdown Hill
row.description: A multi-period archaeological site on an 81-metre chalk hill in West Sussex, featuring a Bronze Age Ram's Hill type enclosure, an Iron Age univallate hillfort refortified c. 270-300 AD, and a major Anglo-Saxon mixed-rite cemetery [1] [2] [3]. The cemetery, discovered in the 1890s, yielded over 200 burials from the 5th-6th centuries AD with an unusual number of glass objects [1] [3]. The site suffered damage from a WWII radar station and the 1987 Great Storm [1].

row.name: Menhir of Patalou
row.description: The Menhir of Patalou is located in the Nisa municipality in the Portalegre District of Portugal, about 5 km from the town of Nisa [1]. The menhir is a megalithic standing stone dating back to the 5th millennium BCE [1]. It is believed to be the second oldest example of a menhir to be identified in Western Europe [1]. The Menhir of Patalou is situated on a gentle east-facing slope, framed by two small hills [1]. Having fallen over in the Chalcolithic era, it was re-erected in 2015, six meters north of its original location [1]. The stone was carved out of granite and has phallic features [1]. Its total height is 4 meters and the maximum diameter is 1.07 meters [1]. The menhir was found in the late 1990s by a hunter, João Francisco Lopes, when he was hunting in the Tapada da Bajanca [1].

row.name: Barbrook One
row.description: Barbrook One is a stone circle on Ramsley Moor in the Peak District [1]. "Barbrook No. 1" is an embanked stone circle [1]. It has one large standing stone (1 metre high) and 11 smaller stones (5 cm to 25 cm high) [1]. The circle has an internal diameter of about 13 metres, and it is surrounded by a rubble bank 3 metres wide [1]. The stone circle stands in a cairn field on Ramsley Moor [1].

row.name: Kintradwell Broch
row.description: Kintradwell Broch (also known as Cinn Trolla) is an Iron Age broch on the coast north of Brora in Sutherland, Highland Scotland [1] [2] [3]. When excavated, the entrance passage was found to be 2.1 m high -- unusually tall for a broch -- and a rock-cut well over 2 m deep with steps was discovered within the tower [1]. Surrounding the broch is an extensive settlement linked by passages to the tower [1].

row.name: Funzie Girt
row.description: Funzie Girt is an ancient wall that was erected from north to south across the island of Fetlar in Shetland, Scotland [1]. The line of the wall, which ran for over 4 kilometres, once divided the island in two almost equal sections [1]. Also known as the Finnigirt Dyke, it has vanished in places at the southern end, although the ruins are clearly visible along much of the uninhabited north of the island [1]. The dyke's original purpose is not known, nor is its relationship to other archaeological sites of a similar age nearby [1]. The name "Funzie Girt" means "Finns' dyke", the Finns being the legendary pre-Norse inhabitants of the islands who were said to possess magical powers [1]. Originally 1 metre wide it begins at the north shore by the cliffs of Muckle Funziegord Geo, crosses an RSPB reserve to the west of Vord Hill, then vanishes near the enclosure of Whilsa Pund [1]. It can be seen again passing the Haltadans stone circle as it heads for the northern shore of Skutes Water [1]. The northern, and most complete section of Funzie Girt has been protected as a scheduled monument since December 1957 [1].

row.name: St Laurence School - Roman Villa
row.description: St Laurence School - Roman Villa is an archaeological site in Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire, England [1] [2]. Minor excavations in 1976 revealed the presence of a Roman villa beneath the school's sports fields [1] [2]. A major excavation in 2003 uncovered Roman-era floor mosaics and walls belonging to the villa complex [1] [3]. The excavations also revealed a stone structure believed to have been part of an early Christian baptistery, suggesting the site may have had later religious significance [1] [4].

row.name: El Tortuguero
row.description: Tortuguero (or El Tortuguero) is an archaeological site in southernmost Tabasco, Mexico which supported a Maya city during the Classic period [1]. The site is noteworthy for its use of the B'aakal emblem glyph also found as the primary title at Palenque [1]. Because of its mid-20th century destruction, little is known about the dynastic lineage of this site [1]. Its history is linked to that of the kingdom of Palenque, as the rulers of Tortuguero used the same emblem glyph as Palenque [1]. Monument 6 from Tortuguero has recently generated discussion as it includes the only known inscription depicting the end of the current 13-Bak'tun era in 2012 [1].

row.name: Hob Hurst's House
row.description: Hob Hurst's House is a Bronze Age barrow on Beeley Moor near Bakewell in Derbyshire [1]. The barrow is in the guardianship of English Heritage and is a Scheduled Ancient Monument [1]. It is situated on Harland Edge above Chatsworth House, near the highest part of Beeley Moor [1]. The barrow was excavated in 1853 by Thomas Bateman, the "Barrow Knight" [1]. The dig found a stone-lined grave containing some scorched human bones plus some lead ore [1].

row.name: Cave of the Guanches
row.description: The Cave of the Guanches, or Archaeological area of the Cave of the Guanches, is an important archaeological site located in the north of the island of Tenerife (Canary Islands, Spain) [1]. The protected archaeological environment is in the municipality of Icod de los Vinos and revolves around the Cave of the Guanches [1]. This archaeological area is where the earliest Guanche autochthonous settlements on the island of Tenerife have been found [1]. It has provided the oldest chronologies of the Canary Islands [1]. These have been dated to the 6th century BCE, according to analysis carried out on ceramics that were found inside [1]. The area was in aboriginal times a village of natural caves and huts (now disappeared), which were located at the top of a cliff, about 125 m above sea level [1].

row.old_value: A 380 BC Lycian tomb whose wall was covered in 152 carved stone panels depicting Greek myths. The entire frieze was removed to Vienna in 1882.
row.new_value: The Heroon of Trysa is the modern name for an ancient tomb, built around 380 BCE in Trysa.

row.old_value: An Inca-era settlement with layers from early Nasca pottery through to Spanish colonial ruins. Each culture left its mark stacked in sequence.
row.new_value: The site presents evidence of human occupation from the Early Intermediate period, including examples of Early Nasca pottery.

row.old_value: A Neolithic earthwork from 4500-2500 BC that has never been excavated. It may be a Saxon boundary ditch, but its true age and purpose remain unknown.
row.new_value: King Lud's Entrenchments is a scheduled monument. The site has not been excavated and its date is unknown.

row.old_value: 900–1470 AD. Chachapoya tombs wedged into a rock cleft in cloud forest, painted red, yellow, black, and white. Closed to all but scientific missions — named for their carved wooden phalluses.
row.new_value: The clay and stone tombs of the complex have wooden roofs and are painted in red, yellow, black, and white colors.

row.old_value: Headland broch on North Ronaldsay separated from the mainland by defensive earthworks. The entrance passage has a guard cell and bar-holes for securing the door against intruders.
row.new_value: The Broch of Burrian is an Iron Age broch located on North Ronaldsay in the Orkney Islands. The Broch of Burrian was excavated by William Traill, proprietor of the island, in 1870 and 1871.

row.old_value: A hilltop with 12 Bronze Age burial mounds dating from 1800 BC and a large Iron Age hillfort. The chalk landscape preserves rare flora alongside the ancient earthworks.
row.new_value: The hill is also the site of a Neolithic causeway camp and barrows; and an Iron Age hill fort.

row.old_value: A Chimu adobe palace from around 900 AD with three terraces covered in zoomorphic and geometric friezes. Linked to the capital Chan Chan during the empire's rise.
A victory pillar at Delphi, originally built by Macedonia but seized and repurposed by Rome after the Battle of Pydna in 168 BC. The conqueror literally put his name on his enemy's monument.
row.new_value: The Monument of Aemilius Paullus was erected in the Sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi shortly after 167 BCE in order to commemorate the Roman victory over King Perseus of Macedon at the Battle of Pydna.

row.old_value: A Paleolithic settlement known for engraved mammoth-ivory bracelets with geometric patterns. Some researchers argue the marks are the earliest known attempt at musical notation.
A Late Neolithic or Bronze Age bowl barrow on Anglezarke Moor, measuring 73 m by 66 m and up to 5.5 m high. Unexcavated and scheduled, it aligns between Great Hill and the Pikestones long cairn.
row.new_value: Round Loaf is a Late Neolithic or Bronze Age tumulus on Anglezarke Moor in the West Pennine Moors near Chorley in Lancashire.

row.old_value: A Harappan-era settlement occupied from 3000 to 1900 BC, just 6 km from the even older site of Mehrgarh. Together they span 7,000 years of continuous civilization.
A 4000-2500 BC dolmen, part of a trio of megalithic tombs clustered in the same area. Each one held generations of burials in a shared stone chamber.
row.new_value: The Anta da Estria, the Anta do Monte Abraão and the Anta da Pedra dos Mouros are collectively known as the Antas de Belas, and were first identified in the 1870s by Carlos Ribeiro.

row.old_value: A small buttress dam in Grândola, built in two phases during Roman occupation. Its rectilinear wall stretched 40 m, supported by six downstream buttresses spaced 2.5 m apart.
row.new_value: The dam was first noted by Father Carvalho Costa in 1712 in his work, Corographia Portugueza.

row.old_value: Built as a Bronze Age burial chamber on Exmoor, it later marked the corner of four parishes simultaneously. Its name evolved from Osmunesburgh (13th c.) to Owlaman's Burrow before settling in 1782.
Built 5th–8th centuries AD on a ridge from the Maya Mountains, Xnaheb's architectural similarities to nearby Nim Li Punit suggest a deliberate founding as a satellite or offshoot center.
row.new_value: The center is built on a ridge of foothills that extends from the Maya Mountains.

row.old_value: A phallic granite menhir from the 5th millennium BC, standing 2.7 metres tall near the town of Nisa. Scholars regard it as the second oldest identified menhir in western Europe.
row.new_value: The menhir is a megalithic standing stone dating back to the 5th millennium BCE.

row.old_value: 5th–7th century AD stupa of mud and baked brick in the Kachho plains of Sindh, standing 15.2 m high. Buddhism coexisted with Hinduism in this region until the 13th century Soomra dynasty.
row.new_value: The Thul Hairo Khan is a Buddhist stupa, built possibly between the 5th and 7th centuries CE near the modern-day town of Johi, in Sindh.

row.old_value: A 5,300-year-old bowl barrow 30 metres across that kept being reused for burial. Anglo-Saxon warriors were later interred in the same mound, 4,000 years after its builders.
row.new_value: The barrow was constructed in the early Bronze Age on the site of a Neolithic settlement, and much later, around the 6th century, it was re-used as an Anglo-Saxon cemetery.

row.old_value: Over 500 standing stones from around 5000 BC spread across two municipalities in Huelva. This 5th–4th millennium BC complex rivals the largest megalithic concentrations in Europe.
row.new_value: The La Torre-La Janera megalithic site is located in the municipalities of Ayamonte and Villablanca in the province of Huelva.

row.old_value: 17.4 metres across externally, 10.5 metres internally — walls still standing over 2 metres around most of the circumference. A scarcement ledge inside once supported an upper timber floor.
row.new_value: Dun Hallin is an Iron Age broch located near the northwest coast of the island of Skye.

row.old_value: A 7th-century Maya city whose ruler Bahlam Ajaw conquered Comalcalco in 649 AD. Its monuments bear the inscription that fueled the 2012 "end of the world" media frenzy.
row.new_value: Monument 6 from Tortuguero has recently generated discussion as it includes the only known inscription depicting the end of the current 13-Bak'tun era in 2012.

row.old_value: A cave tied to the Guanche people, who arrived around 600 BC. The Guanches had no boats — how they reached the islands remains debated.
row.new_value: The area was in aboriginal times a village of natural caves and huts, which were located at the top of a cliff, about 125 m above sea level.

row.old_value: A Romano-Celtic temple active from around 69 AD to the late 4th century. Excavations revealed ritual deposits of bird skeletons paired with coins.
row.new_value: Above Bowleaze Cove, Jordan Hill Roman Temple is a Romano-Celtic ruin with a cemetery of cremations and inhumations and a precinct that held deposits of animal bones, ceramics and coins.

row.old_value: Built 521–515 BC as the winter palace of Darius I on the ruins of an Elamite city. Alexander burned it in 330 BC. A handful of pillars and partial walls survive of one of antiquity’s grandest courts.
row.new_value: At Apadana Castle Shush stood the Palace of Darius in Susa, where the Persian column topped by two bulls was probably developed. Once destroyed by fire and partly restored, little remains.

row.old_value: Ancient drover's road moving cattle from Wales to southeastern markets. Merging with Watling Street at Shrewsbury, it passed through Cannock Chase - a well-worn economic artery used for centuries.
row.new_value: Cattle from North Wales were driven along the Welsh Road to markets in South East England. Its age is not known, yet many lengths follow parish boundaries, hinting at a pre-Roman trackway.

row.old_value: The Broch of Burrian is an Iron Age broch located on North Ronaldsay in the Orkney Islands. The Broch of Burrian was excavated by William Traill, proprietor of the island, in 1870 and 1871.
row.new_value: On a small headland of North Ronaldsay, the Iron Age Broch of Burrian gave up painted pebbles, part of an iron bell of Celtic type and a cross-slab with an ogham inscription.

row.old_value: The barrow was constructed in the early Bronze Age on the site of a Neolithic settlement, and much later, around the 6th century, it was re-used as an Anglo-Saxon cemetery.
row.new_value: Badgers were damaging Barrow Clump, an early Bronze Age bowl barrow in Wiltshire. Digging uncovered many Saxon graves and a bucket-shaped drinking vessel of yew wood bound with bronze.

row.old_value: A Bronze and Iron Age site with continuous occupation, featuring rectangular stone houses from the First Iron Age. Imported Phoenician trade goods show Mediterranean contacts.
row.new_value: On the Ebro's west bank, Late Bronze Age cottages grew into the First Iron Age streets of Barranc de Gàfols: at least 17 households, a fireplace in each, and one building with stone mills.

row.old_value: The Anta da Estria, the Anta do Monte Abraão and the Anta da Pedra dos Mouros are collectively known as the Antas de Belas, and were first identified in the 1870s by Carlos Ribeiro.
row.new_value: At the Anta da Estria, a megalithic dolmen believed to date to 4000-2500 BC, Carlos Ribeiro identified nine raised slabs but no stones that could have formed a roof.

row.old_value: Dun Hallin is an Iron Age broch located near the northwest coast of the island of Skye.
row.new_value: On a steep rocky plateau of Skye above a fertile valley and the sea, the Iron Age broch of Dun Hallin still stands up to 3.8 metres, oval guard cells flanking its entrance passage.
