row.old_value: The center is built on a ridge of foothills that extends from the Maya Mountains.
row.new_value: On a ridge in the foothills of the Maya Mountains lies Xnaheb, one of five primary Maya sites of southern Belize. Shared architectural traits hint it began as an offshoot of Nim Li Punit.

row.old_value: A late-antique defensive wall stretching 1.6 km across a valley to block invaders. Only 336 metres survive, with rooms for defenders built into its western face.
row.new_value: Across the Gailtal valley ran the Hadnmauer, a Late Antiquity barrier from Rattendorf to Jenig. Of its 1.6 kilometres only 336 metres survive, rooms for its defenders still on the west.

row.old_value: Rectangular rather than round, this Bronze Age barrow on Beeley Moor breaks the standard burial mold. Built with 13 stones, only five survive on this exposed moorland edge.
row.new_value: On Harland Edge above Chatsworth House lies Hob Hurst's House, a Bronze Age barrow. In 1853 the Barrow Knight dug in and found a stone-lined grave with scorched human bones and lead ore.

row.old_value: The site presents evidence of human occupation from the Early Intermediate period, including examples of Early Nasca pottery.
row.new_value: Tambo Viejo spreads over approximately 44 hectares of Arequipa: a large rectangular plaza to the north, a labyrinth of structures to the south, and Early Nasca pottery among its traces.

row.old_value: A Late Bronze Age necropolis on Mount Olympus with tombs from the 14th to 12th century BC. Burial offerings in Mycenaean style were found far from Mycenae.
row.new_value: On Mount Olympus lies Spathes, a Late Bronze Age necropolis of 34 partly plundered tombs, where a bronze sword, perfume bottles and stone seals, some with animal motifs, came to light.

row.old_value: Three aligned henges forming a ritual landscape comparable to Salisbury Plain. The complex dates from 3500–2500 BC and includes a cursus and burial sites.
row.new_value: On a plateau above the River Ure, the Thornborough Henges form three almost identical rings, each approximately 240 metres across, with a cursus running beneath the central one.

row.old_value: A Neolithic burial chamber within a hedge bank, with a megalithic chamber and single entrance passage. Part of the original cairn still survives around the tomb.
row.new_value: On a slope above Broadsands Beach, the Broadsands Chambered Tomb now lies in a hedge bank: a Neolithic megalithic chamber that held the fragmentary remains of two adults and a child.

row.old_value: A possible Neolithic henge from 3000 BC, enclosing 7 hectares with a chalk bank and ditch. The River Lea has its source within the surrounding marshland.
row.new_value: Near the prehistoric Icknield Way, Waulud's Bank dates to around 3000 BC, a chalk and gravel bank faced by a wooden stockade. Excavators found pottery, animal bones and flint arrow heads.

row.old_value: Round Loaf is a Late Neolithic or Bronze Age tumulus on Anglezarke Moor in the West Pennine Moors near Chorley in Lancashire.
row.new_value: A landmark on Anglezarke Moor, Round Loaf is an oval mound of earth and small stones raised in the Late Neolithic or Bronze Age. Flakes of flint have been found on its summit.

row.old_value: A Roman east-west road linking north-south routes across a free-draining greensand ridge. It was a planned military route, not a paved-over Iron Age track.
row.new_value: Along a greensand ridge north of the South Downs, the Sussex Greensand Way linked Roman villas and their estates on flint metalling. When in the Roman period it was built is not known.

row.old_value: A 1st-century BC Roman arch originally honoring the alliance between Emperor Augustus and a local Gallic king. Its relief panels depict the treaty scene.
row.new_value: In Susa, the Arch of Augustus opens a single archway framed by four Corinthian columns, built in 9–8 BC to record a renewed alliance between Emperor Augustus and Marcus Julius Cottius.

row.old_value: 6th-century BC Archaic stele from Corfu marking the grave of a warrior killed near the river Arachthos. Its epitaph enumerates his bravery in one of antiquity's earliest surviving verse inscriptions.
row.new_value: Found in 1846 in a Corfu necropolis, the Stele of Arniadas carries a verse epigram in boustrophedon, praising a warrior who fell in battle near ships on the banks of the river Arachthos.

row.old_value: An ancient wall stretching 4 km across the island of Fetlar, dividing it into two nearly equal halves. Its exact date and purpose remain unknown.
row.new_value: Funzie Girt, the Finns' dyke, once ran for over 4 kilometres across the Shetland island of Fetlar, dividing it in two almost equal sections. What it was first built for is not known.

row.old_value: King Lud's Entrenchments is a scheduled monument. The site has not been excavated and its date is unknown.
row.new_value: Unexcavated and undated, King Lud's Entrenchments and The Drift was thought a Saxon boundary ditch, yet aerial photos hint it may belong to a prehistoric boundary running to the Humber.

row.old_value: Built 1700–1550 BC for an obscure 13th Dynasty pharaoh of the turbulent Second Intermediate Period. Every stone of its upper structure was stripped by robbers; only the substructure survives.
row.new_value: In southern Dahshur, the Ameny Qemau Pyramid once stood 35 metres high for an obscure king of the 13th Dynasty. Its stone upper structure was robbed; its damaged substructures remain.

row.old_value: The Thul Hairo Khan is a Buddhist stupa, built possibly between the 5th and 7th centuries CE near the modern-day town of Johi, in Sindh.
row.new_value: Near Johi in Sindh rises Thul Hairo Khan, a Buddhist stupa 50 feet high of mud and baked bricks, built possibly between the 5th and 7th centuries CE, an arched tunnel at its foot.

row.old_value: Eight-metre-diameter Bronze Age entrance grave on the Isles of Scilly, set on a low platform 12 metres across. Directly below lie the remains of the Iron Age village of Halangy Down.
row.new_value: On a steep slope of St Mary's, a roofless entrance leads past a jamb into the burial chamber of Bant's Carn, a Bronze Age entrance grave roofed by four large capstones.

row.old_value: The Monument of Aemilius Paullus was erected in the Sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi shortly after 167 BCE in order to commemorate the Roman victory over King Perseus of Macedon at the Battle of Pydna.
row.new_value: At Delphi, a pillar once meant for a portrait of King Perseus became the Monument of Aemilius Paullus, crowned by a bronze equestrian statue and a frieze of the Battle of Pydna.

row.old_value: A 4th-millennium BC chambered tomb built from local sarsen megaliths. It was dismantled when found in 1822 and the human remains inside were scattered.
row.new_value: Discovered in 1822 and then dismantled, Smythe's Megalith was a long barrow of earth and sarsen stones near Aylesford in Kent, where human remains were laid in its stone chamber.

row.old_value: The dam was first noted by Father Carvalho Costa in 1712 in his work, Corographia Portugueza.
row.new_value: First noted by Father Carvalho Costa in 1712, the Roman Dam of Pego da Moura in Grândola is a small buttress dam built almost entirely of opus incertum, braced by six downstream buttresses.

row.old_value: Headland fort at 60 metres above Hope Cove in Devon, defended inland by a single linear earthwork. Little physical evidence of the structure remains above ground today.
row.new_value: Southwest of Hope Cove, the Devon headland of Bolt Tail once held an Iron Age promontory fort, some 60 metres above sea level and defended from inland by an earthwork. Little of it remains.

row.old_value: A major Neolithic temple sharing design features with the famous Ggantija and Hagar Qim temples. Nearby cart ruts and a dolmen add to the ritual landscape.
row.new_value: Southeast of the Ta' Ċenċ plateau lies Borġ l-Imramma, a major temple-period building sharing some traits of temples like Ħaġar Qim, with cart ruts and a dolmen nearby.

row.old_value: The area was in aboriginal times a village of natural caves and huts, which were located at the top of a cliff, about 125 m above sea level.
row.new_value: Atop a cliff in the north of Tenerife lay a village of natural caves and huts. At the Cave of the Guanches, ceramics found inside have been dated to the 6th century BCE.

row.old_value: A reservoir where a hoard of Bronze and Iron Age weapons was found during construction work. The mix of bronze and iron pieces dates it to the exact transition between the two ages.
row.new_value: Into the lake of Llyn Fawr, in a glacial cirque, went two bronze cauldrons and axeheads, part of a hoard of weapons and tools that appears to have been placed as votive offerings.

row.old_value: A Neolithic cist tomb from 3000-2500 BC with a capstone carried from a nearby river. The burial chamber sits on a small ridge in a city park.
row.new_value: In Phoenix Park near Dublin, a water-worn capstone thought to come from the River Liffey crowns Knockmaree Dolmen, a Neolithic cist found in 1838 when workmen removed its mound.

row.old_value: A four-stone alignment from 1700 BC stretching east to west. Tradition holds it marks the grave of Scéine, wife of the leader of the Milesian invasion.
row.new_value: Four tall slabs, 1.8 to 3 meters high, run east and west: Eightercua Stone Row, thought to date from around 1700 BC and by tradition the burial place of Scéine, wife of Amergin mac Míled.

row.old_value: Cave murals from 1200–900 BC deep underground — the earliest sophisticated painted art in Mesoamerica. The only known example of non-Maya deep cave art on the continent.
row.new_value: In the Grottos of Juxtlahuaca, painted walls show a large bearded man in a black cloak and a red Feathered Serpent with green plumes. A dozen skeletons were found in the Hall of the Dead.

row.old_value: The hill is also the site of a Neolithic causeway camp and barrows; and an Iron Age hill fort.
row.new_value: On White Sheet Hill in Wiltshire, a Neolithic causeway camp and barrows share the ground with an Iron Age hill fort, and a Roman road along it was once the main route through Selwood Forest.

row.old_value: A 32,000-square-metre Iron Age settlement dating to 100 BC — 70 years older than Roman Silchester. It may be the first planned town in Britain.
row.new_value: Duropolis in Dorset is believed to be Britain's first planned town. Remains of 16 Iron Age roundhouses were dug up, and animal skeletons may hint at a belief in hybrid-animal monster myths.

row.old_value: A decorated granite stone from ~100 BC covered in swirling La Tene-style Celtic patterns. The top half is carved; the bottom half was left rough, meant to be buried in the earth.
row.new_value: A curvilinear La Tène style design covers the top half of the Turoe Stone in County Galway, probably from about 100 BC to AD 100. Its religious or ceremonial purposes are lost in time.

row.old_value: 5th–9th century Maya capital near Copán. Abandoned in 822 AD when the Copán kingdom collapsed — one of dozens of satellite cities that fell silent as the Classic Maya world unraveled.
row.new_value: Rastrojón was built on a geological fault just two kilometres from Copán. When the Maya kingdom of Copán collapsed in 822, the site was abandoned, perhaps no longer worth the effort.

row.old_value: Around 3000 BC, hundreds of mysterious stone megaliths were erected in the Lore Lindu highlands. Purpose and builders remain unknown. First recorded by Western observers in 1908 — still no answers.
row.new_value: Statues locals call Palindo and Tarae Roe show faces with brow and nose as one and no mouth: the Bada Valley Megaliths, where lidded burial jars 1.5-2 meters in diameter were found.

row.old_value: Bronze Age cairns sit atop the highest point of Bodmin Moor at 420 metres. The hill shifts from a conical peak to a multi-peaked crest depending on the vantage point.
row.new_value: On the highest point of Bodmin Moor, 1,378 feet up, the summit pile of the Brown Willy Cairns has never been excavated. Folklore suggests an ancient Cornish king may lie entombed underneath.

row.old_value: A 108-metre-long Neolithic stone row of nine megaliths, also known in Cornish as Naw-voz, meaning "the nine sisters." Stones range from 0.8 to 1.4 metres tall.
row.new_value: Nine megaliths, the nine sisters in Cornish, form the Nine Maidens Stone Row, a late neolithic line approximately 108 metres long, aligned towards a moorland stone known as the Fiddler.

row.old_value: A stone circle on Ramsley Moor with one tall standing stone and 11 smaller ones, ringed by a rubble bank. It sits in a broader cairn field dotted with burial monuments.
row.new_value: On Ramsley Moor in the Peak District, in a field of cairns, Barbrook One sets one standing stone and 11 smaller ones in a circle about 13 metres across, ringed by a rubble bank.

row.old_value: A Maya city from 550-830 AD in a remote jungle region. Its carved stelae record royal histories and alliances, including ties to the powerful Calakmul dynasty.
row.new_value: On the banks of the lower Machaquila River lies Machaquila, a ruined Maya city of abundant sculpted monuments, unusual in its region for lacking both a ballcourt and an E-Group.

row.old_value: The Heroon of Trysa is the modern name for an ancient tomb, built around 380 BCE in Trysa.
row.new_value: Raised around 380 BCE in ancient Lycia, the Heroon of Trysa was a tomb whose square outer wall bore a figural frieze of circa 152 plates, brought to Vienna in 1882.

row.old_value: Late Pleistocene burials from a former lakeshore, with over 22 individuals. Among the most robust early skeletal remains found on the continent.
row.new_value: On the rim of a former wetland, the Kow Swamp Archaeological Site held the largest known single population of late Pleistocene human remains, returned in 1990 to the Yorta Yorta people.

row.old_value: 3rd-century BC Thracian burial complex near Sveshtari, where one tomb is linked to Cothelas, king of the Getae. Just metres from this site stands the world-heritage Tomb of Sveshtari.
row.new_value: Near Sveshtari, the Getic Burial Complex holds a Thracian tomb from the beginning of the third century BC and the Omurtag mount, a tomb linked to Cothelas, king of the Getae.

row.old_value: A Maya city from 600-1050 AD with a palace, altar, and a round structure that may be an oven. About 300 structures spread across a 6 km site.
row.new_value: In northeast Yucatan lies Kulubá, a Maya city with a palace 55 metres long, an altar, and a round structure believed to be an oven, amid some 300 smaller structures.

row.old_value: The clay and stone tombs of the complex have wooden roofs and are painted in red, yellow, black, and white colors.
row.new_value: Perched in a high rock cleft of Peru's northern Andean cloud forests, the Chachapoya tombs of Los Pinchudos, of clay and stone under wooden roofs, are painted red, yellow, black and white.

row.old_value: A Roman signal tower built on high ground above the Stanegate road in the early 2nd century AD. It was later absorbed into Hadrian's Wall, with a 2-metre fragment still standing.
row.new_value: On high ground above the Roman Stanegate road, Pike Hill Signal Tower signalled to Gillalees Beacon and Barrock Fell. Built before the nearby walls, it later became part of Hadrian's Wall.

row.old_value: A small circular embanked enclosure, or "round," common to the Iron Age and post-Roman period. Part of the stone rampart still stands 1.6 metres high.
row.new_value: On a ridge above the Lamorna valley, Castallack Round keeps part of a rampart of large stones and slabs. The tithe map of 1840 shows a colonnade of stones leading to an inner enclosure.

row.old_value: A 19-metre Neolithic mound from around 2400 BC, second in height only to nearby Silbury Hill. It was later used as a castle motte, hiding its prehistoric origins for centuries.
row.new_value: Standing 19 metres tall, Marlborough Mound is second in height only to nearby Silbury Hill. It dates from around 2400 BC, the Neolithic period, and its original purpose is unknown.

row.old_value: Set on a 15-metre hill near Bagenkop harbour and dating to 3300–3200 BC, this Funnelbeaker passage grave has a chamber and a separate lateral passageway — a form more common in Germany.
row.new_value: On a hill on Langeland, the Hulbjerg Passage Grave hid flint daggers, amber beads and the bones of 36 adults and 17 children in a separate section of its stone chamber.

row.old_value: Early Formative pyramid complex, 2000–1500 BC. The main temple measures 350 by 300 metres and stands 35 metres tall — one of the largest architectural structures in the ancient Americas of its era.
row.new_value: On the left bank of the Sechín River rises Sechin Alto, its pyramidal Templo 35m high, fronted by five plazas, some with sunken circular courts, in a ceremonial complex from 2000-1500 BC.

row.old_value: Cliff-top broch on Mainland Orkney, 20 metres above sea. External diameter 17 metres; walls 3.5 to 5 metres thick -- the double-skin dry-stone construction typical of the form.
row.new_value: On a cliff-top promontory 20 metres above the sea, the Broch of Borwick keeps walls 3.5 to 5 metres thick. Its finds included combs, a small whale vertebra cup and a stone gaming piece.

row.old_value: A Bronze Age hilltop site with stone cists and burial mounds dating from 3300–500 BC. The beacon summit was a ritual focus for millennia.
row.new_value: On the hilltop of Sancreed Beacon, in Cornwall's Penwith peninsula, lie stone cists and Bronze Age burial mounds, while the western slope keeps the remains of a Bronze Age hut.

row.old_value: An early monastic site with low stone walls and a cross-slab standing stone. Artefacts found here date the community to the early Christian era.
row.new_value: Among low ruined walls in County Kerry, a cross-slab standing stone sits in the middle of the Riasc Monastic Settlement, an early monastic site now a National Monument in state care.

row.old_value: The menhir is a megalithic standing stone dating back to the 5th millennium BCE.
row.new_value: The granite Menhir of Patalou, 4 meters tall, dates back to the 5th millennium BCE and is believed to be the second oldest menhir identified in Western Europe. It was re-erected in 2015.

row.old_value: A Sican complex with 50 identified pyramids built between the 8th and 12th centuries AD. The site sits inside a protected forest sanctuary that still covers the ruins.
row.new_value: Within the Historic Forest Sanctuary of Pómac lies Batán Grande, a complex of 50 identified pyramids once occupied by the Sicán culture, where the Lambayeque first appear.

row.old_value: A 7th-century Maya court whose ancient name was Sak-Nikte', 'White Flower.' For decades, its stunning limestone reliefs appeared on the black market before anyone knew where they came from.
row.new_value: In the 1960s looted Maya reliefs from an unknown city surfaced on the art market. They came from La Corona in Petén, the long-sought Site Q, whose old name seems to have been White-Flower.

row.old_value: Fort built in 79 AD, abandoned in the 90s, then replaced by a smaller fortlet around 105 AD. A civilian settlement grew alongside the second fortlet on the eastern side of Castleshaw Valley.
row.new_value: On Castle Hill above the Castleshaw Valley stood Castleshaw Roman Fort, built circa AD 79. A civilian settlement grew here, yet it lay undiscovered until the 1990s.

row.old_value: The La Torre-La Janera megalithic site is located in the municipalities of Ayamonte and Villablanca in the province of Huelva.
row.new_value: In 2018 a farmer in Huelva set out to plant avocados. The survey that followed has so far revealed 526 standing stones at La Torre-La Janera Megalithic Site, upright or lying on the surface.

row.old_value: A Neolithic cave tomb and a Chalcolithic beehive tomb near the beach. The site represents a rare combination of two distinct prehistoric burial traditions in one place.
row.new_value: The Praia das Maçãs Prehistoric Monument joins an artificial Neolithic cave with a later domed tomb, its chamber approximately 5.5 m across. Arrowheads and cylindrical idols were found.

row.new_value: Little is known of the dynasty of El Tortuguero, a Classic-period Maya city in Tabasco, yet its Monument 6 bears the only known inscription depicting the end of the 13-Bak'tun era in 2012.

A local landowner uncovered Huaca Esmeralda from the sand in 1923; the Chimu pyramid in Trujillo shows relief of fishing nets and fish on two platforms of approximately 65 by 41 meters.
On the Desna River bank, Mezine holds Ukraine's most Paleolithic artifact finds: bracelets engraved with marks possibly marking lunar cycles, and the earliest known meander pattern.
At Nausharo, 6 km from Mehrgarh, a pottery workshop gave up fired and unfired pottery, unworked clay and 12 flint blades or blade fragments, plus copper traces on two blade platforms.
On Exmoor, the turf-covered Bronze Age bowl barrow Alderman's Barrow measures 24 by 22 meters and stands 1.4 meters high. In the 13th century it was called Osmunesburgh.

row.old_value: A local landowner uncovered Huaca Esmeralda from the sand in 1923; the Chimu pyramid in Trujillo shows relief of fishing nets and fish on two platforms of approximately 65 by 41 meters.
On the Desna River bank, Mezine holds Ukraine's most Paleolithic artifact finds: bracelets engraved with marks possibly marking lunar cycles, and the earliest known meander pattern.
At Nausharo, 6 km from Mehrgarh, a pottery workshop gave up fired and unfired pottery, unworked clay and 12 flint blades or blade fragments, plus copper traces on two blade platforms.
